title: Ready for me (Berakhot 58a)
hook: Ben Zoma: Adam labored for bread; I wake and find it ready
carry: all this was done for me
tomorrow: what do you say to a friend you haven't seen in a year?

segments.voice: Yesterday, every mind different: the Wise of secrets, and one first family where no two faces match. Today, the same crowd, seen by one sage at breakfast.

Toast takes about one push of a lever. The bread was just there, in a bag, on the counter. So who baked your bread before you were even awake? Ben Zoma, a sage of the Mishnah, stood looking at a great crowd and answered that question out loud. Blessed is the One who created all these to serve me. It sounds, at first, like a strangely self-centered thing to say.
screen: `ONE PUSH OF A LEVER.` → `BREAD, JUST THERE.` → `ALL THESE, TO SERVE ME?`

segments.voice: Then he explains. Look how hard the first man worked before he ate bread: he plowed, sowed, reaped, bound sheaves, threshed, winnowed, sorted, ground, sifted, kneaded, baked, and only then ate. And I wake up and find it all ready for me. The same for clothes: shearing, washing, combing, spinning, weaving. All of it at my door in the morning. So it isn't bragging. It's counting. Each step behind your bread is a person, and Ben Zoma names them one by one. Then he gives a test. A good guest says: look how much trouble my host went to, and all of it for me. A bad guest says: what trouble? I had one piece of bread, one cup; he did it all for his own family anyway. Here's a neighbor who looks at the same plate. In the Qur'an, Muslims read: "Let man consider his food." And the passage goes on to the rain poured down, the earth split open, the grain made to grow. That's shared: stop, look at what you're eating, and see the work behind it. And one honest difference. Ben Zoma counts the people, the plowers and the bakers, and thanks God for them. The Qur'an passage counts God's own work, the rain, the earth, the grain. Neither erases the other.
screen: `PLOWED, SOWED, REAPED… BAKED.` · `NOT BRAGGING. COUNTING.` · `THE GOOD GUEST, THE BAD GUEST.` · `LET MAN CONSIDER HIS FOOD.` · then, large: `ALL THIS WAS DONE FOR ME.`

segments.voice: Take the last thing you ate and count backward, on your fingers. Who sold it, who drove it, who packed it, who picked or milled it, who grew it. When you run out of fingers, keep going in your head.
screen: `THE LAST THING YOU ATE.` · `COUNT BACKWARD.` · `PAST YOUR FINGERS.`

segments.voice: Ready for me: Ben Zoma waking up to bread that a long line of people made, and blessing God for every one of them.
Said like a good guest: all this was done for me. Thirty-eight of fifty, with thanks.

screen: `DAY 1525 COUNTS.` → `BERAKHOT · 38 OF 50.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT DO YOU SAY TO A FRIEND AFTER A YEAR?`

howItsDone: Jews bless God before and after eating, and in the grace after meals a guest adds a blessing for the host, much like Ben Zoma's good guest.

fork.setup: your aunt hosts the whole family for a holiday. on the drive home your cousin says, "she loves cooking; she'd do it anyway." which guest is your cousin being?
options: a fair guest: if the host enjoys it, there's no trouble to thank.
the bad guest: Ben Zoma's bad guest says the host did it for himself.
a good guest: he noticed she loves it, which is a kind of thanks.
fork.reveal: Ben Zoma's bad guest says, what trouble did the host take? he did it for his own household. the good guest says, all this trouble, for me.

original.note: Hebrew: prepared before me; Ben Zoma wakes to find it all ready.

trapdoor: what you thought: a sage who thought the world revolved around him.
what it means: a sage counting every pair of hands behind his bread, and thanking God like a good guest.
what a scholar hears: Berakhot 58a pairs Ben Zoma's two blessings at the Temple Mount (Wise of secrets; who created all these to serve me) with his good-guest and bad-guest sayings.

chat.meaning: Ben Zoma counted every step behind his bread, plowing to baking, and blessed God for it like a good guest. Thanks gets specific.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 58a (Ben Zoma at the Temple Mount: 'who created all these to serve me'; the labors for bread and a garment; the good guest and the bad guest)

notes: 2026-10-15 v3 (recipe v3): wisdom shape with the unity thread. Shared with Islam, in its own words: Qur'an 80:24 (Pickthall 1930) 'Let man consider his food', with 80:25–27 paraphrased. Honest difference: Ben Zoma counts the human labor behind bread and thanks God for it; the Qur'an passage counts God's own work (rain, earth, grain). No ranking, no 'the same'. Please have an Islam reviewer confirm the Pickthall wording and the paraphrase.

Berakhot 58a paraphrased: the list of labors (plowed, sowed, reaped, bound sheaves, threshed, winnowed, sorted, ground, sifted, kneaded, baked) and the garment list (sheared, washed, combed, spun, wove) follow the Talmud's own lists; confirm the order. The script does not state a count.
Ben Zoma 'a sage of the Mishnah' (a tanna); confirm. The Temple Mount setting is kept as 'a great crowd' in the voice.
howItsDone: the guest's blessing for the host in Birkat ha-Mazon (prescribed in Berakhot 46a) is linked to Ben Zoma's good guest as a likeness, not a historical claim; confirm.
The original-language line (מתוקנין לפני, from "I wake and find all these prepared before me") follows the printed Talmud as best known; confirm spelling and vocalization.
